title: Act V, Scene III

teacherSummary.text: Macbeth, trusting the prophecies, refuses to fear the fleeing thanes or 'the boy Malcolm.' He curses a pale servant who reports ten thousand English soldiers. Aside, he says he has lived long enough: his way of life is fallen 'into the sear, the yellow leaf,' without honor, love, obedience or troops of friends. He insists on putting on his armor. He asks the Doctor to 'minister to a mind diseased'; the Doctor says the patient must minister to himself. 'Throw physic to the dogs; I'll none of it.'

significance: Bravado and despair alternate: Macbeth sees clearly what he has lost but clings to the prophecies. His plea to the Doctor shows he knows his wife's illness is guilt.
discussionQuestions: Why might someone act tough on the outside when they feel hopeless inside?

How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with appearance versus reality?

satQuestions.passage:
Bring me no more reports; let them fly all:
Till Birnam wood remove to Dunsinane,
I cannot taint with fear. What’s the boy Malcolm?
Was he not born of woman? The spirits that know
All mortal consequences have pronounced me thus:
“Fear not, Macbeth; no man that’s born of woman
Shall e’er have power upon thee.” Then fly, false thanes,
And mingle with the English epicures:
The mind I sway by and the heart I bear
Shall never sag with doubt nor shake with fear.
Enter a Servant.
The devil damn thee black, thou cream-faced loon!
Where got’st thou that goose look?
There is ten thousand—
Geese, villain?
Soldiers, sir.
Go prick thy face, and over-red thy fear,
Thou lily-liver’d boy. What soldiers, patch?
Death of thy soul! those linen cheeks of thine
Are counsellors to fear. What soldiers, whey-face?
The English force, so please you.
Take thy face hence.
Exit Servant.
Seyton!—I am sick at heart,
When I behold—Seyton, I say!—This push
Will cheer me ever, or disseat me now.
I have lived long enough: my way of life
Is fall’n into the sear, the yellow leaf;
And that which should accompany old age,
As honour, love, obedience, troops of friends,
I must not look to have; but, in their stead,
Curses, not loud but deep, mouth-honour, breath,
Which the poor heart would fain deny, and dare not.
Seyton!

segments.script: Seyton, Macbeth's last attendant, has a name that sounds like 'Satan' to many readers and directors. Bravado and despair alternate: Macbeth sees clearly what he has lost but clings to the prophecies. His plea to the Doctor shows he knows his wife's illness is guilt. Characterization: Macbeth, defiant and despairing, mocks the servant ("cream-faced loon"), speaks of his "way of life" fallen "into the sear, the yellow leaf." Soliloquy: He longs for "honour, love, obedience, troops of friends." Watch for the prophecies: The Witches' riddling prophecies: notice how each promise shapes what Macbeth hopes, fears and does next.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Canst thou not minister to a mind diseased” slowly and put it in my own words: Macbeth asks the doctor whether he can treat a diseased mind and pluck a sorrow from the memory. Next, craft. I notice the medical language of "minister" and "diseased," applied to guilt and grief. The strongest word is “diseased”: it treats a guilty conscience like an illness of the body. Then, effect. What is Macbeth asking the doctor to do for his wife, and for himself? My answer: Macbeth knows medicine cannot cure guilt; when the doctor says the patient must minister to herself, Macbeth's angry reply shows he is also speaking about his own mind.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Annotate the scene for characterization, soliloquy (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this scene suggest about defiance and despair? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how Act V, Scene III develops the idea of defiance and despair. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of imagery and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) Exemplar: Macbeth's despair shows he knows what his crimes have cost him. When the text says “Canst thou not minister to a mind diseased” (Act V, Scene III, line 2145), it shows this directly. He says his life "is fall'n into the sear, the yellow leaf," and asks the Doctor to "minister to a mind diseased."

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.
